A microprocessor is much like a business. Different departments accomplish specific tasks and communicate with other departments, exchanging data.
INTRODUCTIONM
Both use raw input material to produce a finished product. A microprocessor's finished product is information.
There must always be a department in charge of bookkeeping and data processing.
At some time or another, a business must place its product in storage. Microprocessors are no exception.
Of course, each must have some method of communicating and moving the product from one place to another.
Businesses use the mail system to transport products between locations. Microprocessors have a similar system.

MICROPROCESSOR ARCHITECTURE
Microprocessors process large amounts of data. To accomplish this, the microprocessor must place bits of information into storage devices called registers.
S Z X AC X P X C
DISCUSSION
The condition of the ALU is known as its status. The status register is used to store a binary "word", expressing the status of the ALU.
Each bit (or flag) of the status register represents a specific condition.
S Z X AC X P X C
For example, the contents of this status register shows the "zero" flag as being SET. When the zero flag is SET, it indicates the result of the last arithmetic operation equaled 0.
S Z X AC X P X C
The status register is essential to the microprocessor because it makes branch decisions. For example, suppose you want to branch to another part of your program if 2 numbers are equal.
To make this decision, the computer must subtract the two numbers. If a zero is given, the zero flag is set.
S Z X AC X P X C

General purpose registers are also used for temporary storage.
The general purpose (GP) registers store one data word each. The length of a data word depends on the microprocessor.
An eight bit microprocessor will have an eight bit GP register.
A sixteen bit microprocessor will have two 8 bit GP registers paired.
Retrieving information from an external source (floppy disks) is more time consuming than accessing temporary data located within GP registers.
General purpose registers can be addressed with fewer clock pulses and less bytes.
An accumulator is a register the ALU uses as a Operand..

Some microprocessors are able to link two GP registers together. The registers are then treated as one double length register.
Register pairs are useful for storing memory addresses and large data values. Each register pair is named with a letter or letters such as A, B or C.
Individual one word registers might be named "register AL" (low word of register pair A) or "register AH" (high word of register pair A).

Address registers access the location of data in memory. They are connected to the address bus and are sometimes twice the length of the processor word size.

PROCESSOR WORD - The processor word is a set of binary digits or bits treated as a unit. Modern microprocessors have words that are in multiples of 8 bits (8 bits = 1 byte). For example, the Intel 8086 microprocessor chip uses 16 bit words and the Intel 8085 uses 8 bit words.
DEFINITION
Address registers enable a specific Input/Output port. The port's address is stored in an address register and used by the control unit whenever data is moved to or from the address.
The program counter contains the address of the next instruction to be executed. This register makes it possible for the microprocessor to execute instructions in the proper sequence.
The stack register is a block of memory in which data is stored as: Last In, First Out (LIFO).

For example, the last tennis ball stored in a can will have to be the first one removed. The stack pointer (a special register that holds the beginning address of the stack register) automatically adjusts to the next available location in the stack...
The process of loading the stack is called pushing and the process of reading from the stack is called popping.
These commands make the programmer's job easier. The programmer can instruct the microprocessor to push or pop data in or out of the stack without knowing the address.
This command is important when the program is branched away and we don't know how the branch will affect the data in the registers.
The contents of the data registers must be stored before the branch.
For example: Step 1 - The contents of register A are stored in the stack. After this instruction, stack location 1000 contains 1101 (the contents of A).
The stack pointer increments to 1001, the next available address location.
Step 2 - Stack location 1001 contains1111 (contents of B) and the stack pointer contains 1010. The address of the next available location.
Step 3 - The subroutine which may change the content of A and B is executed. The original content of A and B are no longer valid.
Steps 4 and 5 will restore the original contents of registers A and B.
Step 4 - Decrements the stack pointer, then it transfers the content of that stack location into B.
Step 5 - Also decrements the stack pointer, then transfers the contents into A.
Note, after all the steps have been executed, the contents of A and B are the same as their original value.

PHYSICAL CONFIGURATION
Originally, the PC/XT was configured to operate with 1M of memory. 512k was reserved for the system, and the other 512k was reserved for user programs..
DISCUSSION
In fact, DOS had the capability to perform read/write operations to the entire 1M, but was only able to load programs into the 512k that had been established as Conventional Memory, the user memory.
Shortly after that, IBM decided that the 512k reserved for the system was excessive and that system requirements could be sufficiently maintained using only 384k.
This boosted the user area of memory to 640k. At the time, the 640k that DOS could directly manage appeared astronomically large.
It seemed nearly inconceivable that programs would ever be written that might require more than 640k. That theoretical boundary became known as the 640k memory barrier.

Once the AT-type systems were introduced, the original 1M of memory was stretched out to 16M for the '286 and as far as 4G for the '386DX, '486 and Pentium systems. The Pentium P6 processors stretch the boundary to 64G!
RESERVED
ORIGINAL 1M
PENTIUM P6
EXTENDED MEMORY (XMS)
All memory beyond the original 1M is considered Extended Memory (XMS). XMS stands for Extended Memory Specification..

Unfortunately, the "ins and outs" of extended memory are not quite that simple. In order to facilitate an understanding of how Extended Memory is accommodated in various computer systems, some modes of operation need to be defined. Virtual Real Mode ual Real Mode ode ode
DEFINITION
REAL MODE - A mode available in all 8086-compatible processors that enables compatibility with the original 8086. In this mode, RAM storage is limited to 1M.

PROTECTED MODE - This mode is available in all '286 or '386 - compatible processors. In this mode, RAM storage is extended to 16M ('286) and 4G ('386DX >). This mode also allows restricted protection levels to be set to trap software crashes and control the system.
DEFINITION

VIRTUAL REAL MODE - This mode is available in all '386-compatible processors and permits RAM storage up to 4G. Further, individual real mode compatible sessions can be set up and maintained separately from each other.
DEFINITION
Extended Memory Specification was developed in 1987 and specified how programs would use extended memory.
Before XMS, cooperation between program applications that placed the processor in the protected mode and used extended memory was not ensured.
Multiple programs were unable to know what the other was doing with the extended memory, because they were unable to see that memory while in the real mode.
HIMEM.SYS works with programs that understand the XMS protocol by controlling all extended memory and issuing chunks of it to programs as it is needed.
HIMEM.SYS

This enables several programs that use extended memory to operate together under DOS on the same system. XMS prevents a program from trying to acquire a block of memory being used by another program..
The UMA (upper memory area) consists of the reserved 384k on an XT system and the first 1M on AT-type systems. This upper memory provides blocks of RAM used for the system...
One block is reserved for the monitor and is called Video RAM. Another block is reserved for the Adapter BIOS. The last block is set aside for the Motherboard (System) BIOS.
In most cases, there are blocks in the UMA that are not actually being used by the system.
Device Drivers & Memory Resident Programs

For '386 > systems, programs like Memmaker, Ramboost and QEMM will take the unused portions of the UMA and load them with device drivers and memory-resident programs. This frees up otherwise unaccessible user memory..
The HMA (High Memory Area) is roughly the first 64k at the beginning of the first 1M of Extended Memory.
RESERVED
ORIGINAL 1M
PENTIUM P6
EXTENDED MEMORY (XMS)
Like the UMA, it can be used to load device drivers and memory-resident programs in order to free up space in conventional memory.
On systems that operate with DOS 5.0 or higher, this area is particularly important because DOS will load about 45k of program instructions into this area by using DOS's XMS driver HIMEM.SYS.
When this is done, the Config.Sys file will have the line "DOS=HIGH" added. HIMEM.SYS (or an equivalent driver) controls the use of this area.
This area of memory can be accessed because of an oversight
(a boo-boo) when the 80286 was developed..
Memory addresses in Intel microprocessors are stipulated by an overlapping segment and offset.

The 8088/8086 has only 20 address lines (A0 - A19). So, if an address segment FFFF (specifying an actual address of FFFF0 which is 16 bytes shy of the first 1M) is added to an offset of FFFF (equaling 64k) the end result is::

Address 10FFEF can't be achieved with only 20 address lines. The 8088/8086 processors don't quite know what to do with an address that large and so they leave off the MSD (most significant digit) which results in an address of 0FFEF...
This effectually causes the address to wrap around and end up 16 bytes from the end of the first 64k of the first 1M.
RESERVED
ORIGINAL 1M
PENTIUM P6
EXTENDED MEMORY (XMS)
The 80286> processors, when operating in the real mode, are supposed to emulate the 8088/8086 exactly, limiting the processors to 20 address lines.

The aforementioned oversight, however, left address line A20 (the 21st address line) active. This allowed the processor to achieve the address without the wrap around effect, resulting in an address that was 16 bytes less than the first 64k of the second megabyte..
This portion of memory should not have been accessible except in the protected mode.
IBM engineers were well aware of this "bug" in the '80286 processor.

So, when they designed the original AT, they took some unused pins on the keyboard controller and devised them in such a way that the controller would turn on or off the A20 line depending on whether the processor was operating in the real or protected mode.
This allowed the '286 to operate in the real mode exactly as if it were an 8088/8086 processor.

Programmers at Microsoft, realizing the potential, devised a method of commanding the keyboard controller to turn on the A20 line for the sole purpose of using the "bug" as a benefit of accessing the first 64k of extended memory, without having to switch into the protected mode..
This was accomplished with HIMEM.SYS. When it was all over and done, a new category of memory was created called: High Memory.

Prior to Extended Memory, Expanded Memory Specification (EMS) was used.
Expanded Memory is not accessed the same as Conventional and Extended Memory; that is, it cannot be directly addressed by the processor.
In order for an Expanded Memory address to be accessed, it must go through a 64k window in Upper Memory.
EXTENDED MEMORY
RESTRICTED

Expanded memory is a segment-switching operation, very much like a swap file operation. The major difference is that Expanded Memory is segment-switching (swapping) chunks of RAM where swap file operations borrow chunks of Hard Disk space and utilize it as if it were RAM...
Expanded Memory requires an EMS board which has numerous 64k segments in addition to switching and mapping hardware. The EMS board's home address is the 64k segment (window) in Upper Memory...
As that segment is filled with data, it is rotated by the EMS board and a new empty 64k segment is then available.
EXTENDED MEMORY
RESTRICTED

The disadvantage of EMS operations is that only one segment can be utilized at one time. For this reason it is slow and inefficient and, for the same reason, the segments are used to hold data rather than program files...
Due to the fact that EMS was devised with 8-bit processors in mind, the system is nearly extinct today.
The speed with which RAM can be accessed has, over the years, remained fairly constant...
Microprocessor speeds, on the other hand, have been increasing at an impressive rate.
So while processors are trying to acquire and manipulate data at much faster speeds, they are not able to access RAM any faster than they were able to when their own speeds were far less.
To get around this bottleneck, caches are used. A cache is basically very high-speed memory.
Typically; dynamic RAM has an access time of 70-80 nanoseconds, most L1 (internal caches) can be accessed in less than 10 nanoseconds.
With the 486 and Pentium series processors, having caches is an opportunity for them to strut their stuff. The CPU has no wait time because the cache can keep up with the CPU completely.
This, of course, is in contrast to conventional RAM which would cause the CPU to wait while code and data are being accessed.
L2 caches (those external to the processor) are not quite as fast as L1, but still far faster than conventional RAM.
The P6 processor has taken this a step further and incorporated an L2 cache on-board. While it is a separate piece of silicon, it is directly hard-wired to the processor itself and is contained
The L2 cache in the P6 is considerably faster than normal L2 caches.
When the 80486 processor was developed it came with an on-board cache controller with an internal (Level 1) cache of either 8k or 16k cache memory.
The Pentium has two, independent, 8k Level 1 caches and the cache controller circuitry on the processor die.

LOGICAL CONFIGURATION
An understanding of memory before it has been logically allocated in a computer system is advantageous to learning how it is integrated into the computer.
DISCUSSION

There are two primary forms of memory: RAM & ROM. Both of these forms are manufactured in a variety of ways and, hence, have modified characteristics, most of which (from an operative standpoint) are subtle and too insignificant to dwell on. We will first discuss ROM..
ROM is an acronym for Read-Only-Memory, which is to say that information stored in ROM can be read but NOT written to.
The data programmed into it is normally done by the manufacturer or by a special process prior to the chip's installation. Data stored in a ROM IC is commonly referred to as "firmware"..
ROM is considered non-volatile memory because information stored in it will remain there without any power source. This, in contrast to RAM, where once power is removed, all information is lost...
There are certain programs that a computer must have in order to operate once power has been applied. These programs are stored in ROM and are called the system's BIOS.
BIOS stands for Basic Input/Output System and allows the computer to communicate with its peripherals such as the keyboard and monitor.

ROM is manufactured in four functional categories: ROM, PROM, EPROM and EAROM (also called EEPROM). While, as an end product, they perform the same function, the way in which they are programmed and, in some cases, re-programmed varies...
The basic ROM chip is programmed by the manufacturer through a masking process that cannot be changed.
Since the programming is a one shot deal, these IC's are normally used in applications where the end item is sold in large volumes. ROM IC's are less expensive than the other categories.
For the IC manufacturer to mask-in different programs for every end item application was an expensive operation, the cost of which was passed on to the end item manufacturer.
This was the driving force behind the development of the PROM. PROM's are programmable ROM's.
The chips can be produced quickly and in large quantity because the chip manufacturer doesn't need to pre-program the IC's for the makers of whatever application they are sold for.

In this case, say a toy manufacturer buys a large quantity of these chips and programs them electrically using a device called a PROM Programmer. Their major disadvantage is that PROMs, like ROMs, can only be programmed once..
Due to the one time programming disadvantage of the PROM, EPROM's were developed.
The Erasable Programmable Read-Only-Memory (EPROM), as the name suggests, can have its original program erased and then be re-programmed as often as desired.

The only major disadvantage to EPROMs is that the UV light will erase the entire program, not just a small portion of it.
The aforementioned disadvantage of the EPROM was eliminated by the development of the Electrically Alterable Read-Only-Memory (EAROM) or Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only-Memory (EEPROM).

This memory device can be programmed, erased and re-programmed just as the EPROM. The advantage for this category of ROM is that the IC's do not need to be removed from the circuit to be erased and re-programmed..

Further, particular portions of the programming can be erased without destroying the entire program. This makes the EAROM far more versatile than its predecessors. The only disadvantage is that, as might be expected, they are more expensive.
The next form of memory is Random Access Memory (RAM). The term RAM is actually a misnomer. Random access means that the time required to access any location in memory is the same.
Since this characteristic of RAM is also found in ROM, the name really doesn't differentiate between the two forms of memory.
What makes RAM so different from ROM is that the user can write to RAM not just read from it.
When you listen to people discussing computer systems or read the feature of a particular system when shopping for a computer, you will likely hear or read references to the computer's memory.

In most cases, the references are to RAM. As a general rule, the more RAM a computer has, the faster and smoother it will operate. This is particularly true with programs that are graphic intensive, like CAD programs for example...

As was previously mentioned, any information stored in RAM when power is removed from the system will be destroyed. This makes RAM a volatile form of memory.
The memory cells of RAM are either STATIC or DYNAMIC.......
Static RAM stores information in flip flops, which means that any value stored in the cell will remain there so long as power is applied to the chip.
STATIC RAM STORAGE
Dynamic RAM memory cells are constructed using capacitors which store a charge. Like any capacitor, it will, over time (several milliseconds), lose that charge unless it is refreshed.
DYNAMIC RAM STORAGE
The refresh process in Dynamic RAM is accomplished by reading a sequence of address locations in RAM within a specified time frame, normally two milliseconds.

As the addresses are read, the capacitors are recharged, thus re-writing the exact same data onto the memory location. Because flip flops are more complex circuits than capacitors, Static RAM is more expensive..
Static RAM is often referred to as SRAM and Dynamic RAM is often referred to as DRAM.
